headline: A Bloomberg Opinion columnist argues that Blackstone's AI data-centre investments look shaky after public investors balked at similar companies, among them a failed share sale by Firmus in Australia.
score_reason: Pool 6 kept: the column was read in full and its two news points are checkable; it is one columnist's opinion.
importance_line: What changed is a columnist's argument that stock-market investors are turning cool on AI data-centre firms, which matters first to savers and pension holders whose funds lend to or own them, then to the private-credit lenders and to Blackstone, then to the developers that need the money, and the doubt is that it is one columnist's opinion resting on two weak listings, not proof that the deals will lose money.
summary: Bloomberg Opinion columnist Shuli Ren writes that public investors are pushing back on "neoclouds", companies that buy AI chips and lease the computing power to AI developers, citing the failed share sale last week of Firmus, the Sydney data-centre operator in which Blackstone owns 6.7%, and news on Tuesday 13 Oct 2026 that AirTrunk, the Australian data-centre operator Blackstone bought in 2024, is delaying a planned Singapore property-trust listing. She argues that investors now ask when such companies break even, not how large their order backlogs are, pointing out that CoreWeave, a leading neocloud, is expected to make $7.6 billion in earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation this year but plans capital spending of up to $39 billion, and that Blackstone, the $1.3 trillion asset manager, still has to sell its stakes, with AirTrunk and Lambda both planning to list in 2027.
notes: Opinion column, read in full in the Livemint copy; link kept to the Bloomberg original. The Firmus size differs between the column ($30 billion ask) and Reuters ($5 billion IPO), so no figure is printed for it.
